tickets.title: Deployment skeleton
tickets.deliverable: Single Docker release, PostgreSQL migration, readiness check, home Compose, Render Blueprint and Google profile from §7.
tickets.acceptance: Start from an empty home installation. Restart without losing the fixture record. Validate the Compose/Blueprint definitions and Google configuration in CI. Record separate rehearsal status for each hosted profile. A paid staging deployment runs only when the family chooses it.
tickets.context: B0.1 serves a simple status response and is the recommended first assignment.

slices.title: Serve a health response
slices.work: Create the smallest Rust workspace with an Axum router and a binary that binds the configured port. Add a loopback HTTP integration test.
slices.pass_case: GET /healthz returns 200 and a status-only body from the running binary.
slices.adverse_case: An unknown route stays unknown. Logs and the response contain no connection strings.
slices.model: GPT-6 Luna for a bounded implementation or test
slices.suggested_paths: Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, crates/fieldbook/src/ and its router integration test
slices.verify: Run cargo test --workspace --locked, start the actual binary, then request /healthz and an unknown route on loopback.

slices.title: Persist the first migration
slices.work: Add SQLx migrations on PostgreSQL 16, schema-aware /readyz, a non-root release image and a home Compose profile with persistent data.
slices.pass_case: Insert a fictional record, restart app and database, and retrieve the same ID. The ready response is 200.
slices.adverse_case: With the database unavailable or the schema behind, /readyz reports unavailable while /healthz still serves.
slices.model: GPT-6.2 Sol for the integration or review
slices.suggested_paths: migrations/, crates/fieldbook/src/storage/ and SQL-backed integration tests
slices.verify: Run cargo test --workspace --locked with an isolated PostgreSQL 16 database. Inspect committed rows and original file hashes where relevant.

slices.title: Describe all three hosts
slices.work: Add render.yaml and deploy/google with private media, secret references, migration and a readiness probe. Use the same image on every profile.
slices.pass_case: Validate Compose, Blueprint and Google configuration locally or in CI and record each result separately.
slices.adverse_case: Reject durable media on an ephemeral path. A configuration check cannot count as a paid-host rehearsal.
slices.model: GPT-6.2 Sol for the integration or review
slices.suggested_paths: deploy/, compose.yaml, render.yaml and the matching command or runbook
slices.verify: Run docker compose --env-file .env.example config --quiet and the relevant profile-specific checks. Record actual and configuration-only runs separately.

tickets.title: Pretotypes and cumulative prototypes
tickets.deliverable: Start each new project with a pretotype. Save predictions and observations separately. Link each prototype version to one or more observed trials and the learner’s rationale.
tickets.acceptance: Create three pretotypes and two overlapping prototypes, reuse a missed observation in both, retrieve links in both directions, and reject unobserved or foreign sources atomically.
tickets.context: Start at project creation and keep hypotheses, observations and build decisions distinct. The same pretotype can guide several working versions.

slices.title: Start the project with its first trial
slices.work: Extend the normal project-create command to insert the first draft in the same transaction. Implement successive save-plan and record-observation commands. Use a human-authored plan, prediction, true observation date, learner attribution and expected revision.
slices.pass_case: A new project returns a root and exactly one pretotype. A prediction exists before the user records the result.
slices.adverse_case: An exact retry creates one root and one draft. An older imported project opens with empty trials. A task tick cannot produce evidence.

slices.title: Commit cumulative evidence links
slices.work: Persist addressed observation revisions, prototype versions, rationale, test target and project-scoped many-to-many source rows. Authorize all body/path IDs before writing. Return forward and reverse links.
slices.pass_case: Three observed pretotypes allow V1 with P1/P2 and V2 with P2/P3. P2 retains one identity. A follow-up build pins the specific source revisions it selected.
slices.adverse_case: Reject drafts, duplicate or cross-project sources and a stale expected revision without committing a partial version. Replay an accepted request after checking current authorization.

slices.title: Walk from an observation to each build
slices.work: Open the first pretotype from New project. Display labels, plan/observe actions, a checkbox list with actual observations, a rationale and build test. Let an observed source open every build it informed.
slices.pass_case: A learner can cite a miss and an unclear trial, start two alternatives and create a version with one additional observation. Use only the keyboard for one pass.
slices.adverse_case: An empty state explains what to try. A suggestion or checkbox does not count as a real observation. Declined or parked projects stay findable.

tickets.title: Project Failure Résumé and revival

tickets.acceptance: Feature a missed prediction and a real unexpected build setback, remove and restore a selection, print one project, and revive a trial without changing its original observation.
tickets.context: Keep a per-project, learner-curated record of real setbacks. Preserve history through feature, unfeature, print and revival.

slices.title: Select setbacks and render one project

slices.pass_case: Re-adding an entry returns one selection. A build that otherwise worked can appear because an unexpected failure was actually recorded.
slices.adverse_case: Sample results, another project, and unselected or inaccessible evidence produce no résumé content or counts.

S1: At the next available computer, Anush writes, “I lined up the left edges so the pieces were easier to compare.” He can leave the project blank.
The entry saves without a file. A parent can add a photo later under their own name. The activity date can be different from the date they uploaded it.
S2: He saves the failed run with a condition and result. On a later day he links a second run, changes one parameter, and credits the teammate who built the chassis.
The project shows both attempts in order. “My part,” “Help I used,” and “What happened” stay distinct.
S3: A teacher, friend, or parent notices something
A guardian records what a club sponsor saw, the observation date, and whether it is a quote or a paraphrase. A friend can be identified simply as “a club member.”
The card reads, for example, “Club sponsor · paraphrased by parent.” The student’s own reflection stays in its own field.
S4: He links a math-club entry about trying two explanations to a robotics entry about trying two turn settings. He adds, “I kept everything else the same to compare the results.”
The skill view shows both dated examples and his reason for connecting them. Each moment still has one original record.
S5: Friday is busy, or he hit a dead end
He picks one moment, sees last week’s next step, and chooses whether to try it, change it, or let it go. He can skip the week.
The outcome and his next small experiment are available at the next check-in. A missed week creates no backlog.
S6: He compares two ways to plan a camp meal, or archives a short dated music-practice clip. He describes what he could do alone and what someone showed him.
Everyday independence, creative practice, and service use the same capture screen. The family can keep them private indefinitely.
S7: Together they choose two moments, one student takeaway, and optionally an attributed observation cleared for inclusion. They preview the exact one-page record.
The family keeps a dated snapshot. Editing the underlying project later leaves the saved edition readable as it was.
S8: A mentor offers a short conversation
Anush selects a failed turn, its improved test, and one question he wants to ask. His parent checks which details can travel.
A one-page Mentor Brief opens with the question and gives the mentor enough context to respond. Unselected notes stay private.
S9: A later scholarship, internship, research program, or college asks for a sample
He starts from the recipient’s actual prompt, finds two relevant moments, and checks what he contributed and which source files are available.
In the first implementation the Mentor Brief can serve as a starting sheet. Later audience templates can arrange the same evidence around the actual request.
S10: Interests change, or the family moves the app
A guardian adds “Field science,” retires an old skill from new forms, makes a backup, and restores it on a clean instance.
Existing entries, skill links, saved pages, and stored photos survive. A link to a recording still identifies its outside source.
S11: A club visit, Scout outing or family memory
He marks whether he attended, hosted, taught, helped or watched. A photo and a sentence can finish the entry.
He can find his first time teaching and his favorite campout without adding a skill or outcome.
S12: He optionally records event, team or individual role, outcome or personal best. A parent uploads the teacher’s letter, original photo and short demo.
The result, the child’s reaction and the recognition are distinct. A relative can comment on a selected highlight.
S13: He keeps the game file, demonstration and the version he tested. He records one idea AI helped with and the choice he made himself.
The work still opens from a saved copy after a project link changes. A coach can suggest one experiment when requested.
S14: A private reflection and a selected audience
Anush saves his disappointment to the diary and shares a separate family highlight. A parent later uses visible, recorded access when necessary.
The learner sees the access history. Each relative sees precisely the selected entry and files.
S15: The photo and words arrive on different days
A guardian saves the fraction-strip photo under their own name. On the shared computer, Anush links it to his moment or leaves it in Family photos to match.
There is one original asset, two distinct contributions and no need for both devices at once.
S16: One idea becomes a different kind of project
From a fraction lesson he borrows a rhythm, combines it with his saved Scratch idea, tests it on paper, and records what the test changed.
The map and its keyboard list show both sources, his reason, the next small action and his observation.
S17: Anush builds a part of his own Fieldbook
On fictional data he writes a Rust rule to choose a new field and a Svelte control to reveal its explanation.
A reproducible test and one working screen show what he built. He can journal his implementation as a project.
S18: Select a saved idea, add a child, select the new child and split it into smaller parts. Move one existing part into the appropriate group.
Each idea has one home in the ordered outline, and references in other branches still open the same idea.
S19: Two parts can be built separately
Agree on what the beat-pattern maker will give the display. Give the display a sample now, then connect the real output and check both parts together.
The two test results have separate labels. A change to the agreement shows which checks must be revisited.
S20: A persuasive essay grows from a club experience
Plan the reason and its source in Fieldbook, write the body first in Google Docs, and reread the essay there.
The ordered plan, evidence and reverse-outline notes stay with the project. An optional dated PDF preserves one finished draft.
S21: A proud moment predates the app
A parent records an earlier tournament, its activity date, Anush’s role and the reported result. Anush adds his own recollection. A teacher’s PDF can come later.
One portfolio item links to the source moment. Readers can distinguish the event date, recording date, student voice and teacher evidence.
S22: Music, math and coding share one project
Open Graph from a fraction lesson, split the game into branches, and connect the rhythm maker’s output to the display’s input.
The same selected idea, outgoing agreement and incoming evidence are available in Graph and List. Changing a tested interface identifies the affected checks.
S23: Today’s experiment becomes a new achievement
After an actual trial, Anush records what happened and chooses Add to portfolio. He may add another project or skill the observation supports.
One dated source remains attached to the chosen highlight. A proposed idea, a sample run or a checked box alone produces zero portfolio items.
S24: Anush will be away from the computer
Print an ordered checklist for a project or one branch. Cross off steps on paper, add a thought and later enter the marks he wants to keep.
The same item code identifies each step after a rename or reorder. Saving twice creates no new work or evidence.
S25: Several small tests guide two builds
Run three pretotypes, then select P1 and P2 for one version and P2 and P3 for another. Write what each version does with the evidence.
Open P2 from either version and see one unchanged observation and both destination builds.
S26: A failed attempt becomes a point of pride
Feature an actual missed prediction and an unexpected build failure, print the project’s Failure Résumé, then revive one idea under a changed condition.
The first result, learner’s words and original date remain visible beside the linked new attempt.
